## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.31134.017](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.31134.017)

In the interests of transparency, eLife includes the editorial decision letter and accompanying author responses. A lightly edited version of the letter sent to the authors after peer review is shown, indicating the most substantive concerns; minor comments are not usually included.

Thank you for submitting your article "Encoding Sensory and Motor Patterns as Time-Invariant Trajectories in Recurrent Neural Networks" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, one of whom is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors, and the evaluation has been overseen by Richard Ivry as the Senior Editor. The reviewers have opted to remain anonymous.

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

This manuscript reports a computational study in which a recurrent neural network was trained to categorize spatio-temporal input stimuli and produce spatio-temporal patterns as responses. More specifically, the study used spoken digits as input stimuli, and transcriptions of these digits as outputs. The authors show that the trained network is robust to variations in the inputs and to external perturbations. In particular, they show that the network generalizes to untrained utterances of digits, and when trained on utterances of different length is able to deal with temporal stretching and compression of the stimuli. These results are interpreted in terms of stimulus-elicited neural trajectories, which show a degree of temporal invariance.

The paper is clearly a well-described, well-thought out computational experiment in artificial recurrent neural networks. However, all reviewers felt that its biological conclusions remain unclear. On a computational level, we know from much work in machine learning, where the task that the authors consider would be called a sequence-to-sequence task, that recurrent neural networks are indeed able to instantiate such computations (e.g., Sutskever et al., 2014). We also know, as the authors themselves report, that alternative mechanisms for dealing with time warping exist.

Accordingly, just the fact that the trained networks could solve the task is not in and of itself a strong biological finding. There are three ways the reviewers feel the paper could be improved, in order of importance:

1) What is the novel biological insight offered by the study? At present there is little detail on this. One prediction appears in the text: "Specifically, the observation that slower stimuli yield trajectories with larger curvature radii implies that the neural population activity should exhibit larger fluctuations in their firing rates in response to slower stimuli". However, in order for that to be a true prediction one would need to show that this is a necessary, or at least generic property, for instance by studying multiple different types of tasks involving temporal warping, or showing somehow that without this increase in curvature radius the trajectories cannot be learned. Moreover, the effect size for this prediction shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1D appears quite mild (25% increase in range across the full span of warping). both generally and at the mechanistic level.

2) What is the extent and nature of the generalization that these networks are capable of. The authors demonstrate some interpolation and extrapolation of time-warping as well as an ability to reject certain kinds of noise. A stronger test might be for instance whether a network given a training set with naturally spoken examples all time-warped to the same duration, would still be able to generalize to stimuli of different durations?

3) How generic are the results? Is this approach different from previous generic deep learning results? Can the authors describe better the underlying mechanism, Can they convincingly say for instance that the mechanism that they describe in Figure 8 for example is typical, or necessary? That it would remain the same given different choices about training paradigms, etc.

We realize that these are difficult points to address (especially point three). We feel these will be the best ways to strengthen the biological conclusions of the paper, even if a completely full answer cannot be achieved.

To help you in addressing these three main concerns, please find below more detailed reviewer remarks, culled from the original review. Please don't feel you have to address each of these as separate points, I add them here to help you understand in more detail the three main points to be addressed which we listed above.

Major concerns:

1) The network was trained in two steps in which the recurrent weights were trained and then the output weights were trained. I understand the rationale as it is stated in the main text. My question is whether this two-step training is necessary. In a biological case, the network would likely not be trained in such a way. Training would happen presumably all at once based only on the correctness of the output. It would be interesting to show how the network performs when the recurrent and output weights are trained simultaneously. What are the main differences in functionality the network can achieve? Also, a little more text on the rationale for the training procedure would be helpful to reader in the main text.

2) One of the main novelties of the paper is the temporal invariance of the network. The authors state that other models have been developed that can also account for temporal invariance. However, these other models are not fully introduced, forcing the reader to go to the literature to make a comparison. It would be helpful if the text contained a longer introduction to other models and a discussion of how, in functional terms and experimental predictions, the new model presented here compares to and differs from the published models cited in the text.

3) The paper emphasizes the idea of generalizing to different speeds of stimuli. The current results show that when trained on stimuli of different durations, generalization can occur. However, it is unclear if this generalization is a natural consequence of encoding stimuli as trajectories or requires training on different durations. That is, if the network is given a training set with naturally spoken examples all time-warped to the same duration, would the network be able to generalize to stimuli of different durations? The answer to this question helps the reader better understand the scope of the generalization that can occur.

4) How does the performance of the network differ for things like generalization, robustness to noise, etc. as a function of the size of the network? Different figures seem to use different size networks (n = 2100 in Figure 3 and n = 4000 in Figure 1), but it was not immediately clear how the network size was chosen.

5) One weakness of the paper is that the extent of mechanistic exploration of the RNN and experimental predictions is rather limited, at least in my opinion. I do not have specific suggestions for how to improve on this point. One possibility is further examination of the recurrent weight matrix to look for specific structure and dynamics that could generate additional experimental predictions. Given that I do not have specific questions here, I do not expect that something must be done in this area. I simply note this point because the impact of the paper will be enhanced if more mechanistic insight into how the RNN functions or into experimental predictions could be added.

6) The relation between this work and the substantial progress in deep learning on general sequence-to-sequence tasks (for example, "Sequence to sequence learning with neural networks" by Sutskever et al., 2014 and the dozens of subsequent papers that built upon it) is unclear. Most of these works in deep learning use backpropagation through time (BPTT) to train their networks, an algorithm which is conceptually very distinct from their tamed chaos method. Given the excellent track record of BPTT on many real-world sequence-to-sequence tasks, it seems that the point that the brain can use recurrent dynamics to solve such tasks is already evident. Perhaps the authors feel their approach is more appropriate in some way? If so, it would be important to compare the performance of the tamed chaos method with that of BPTT on more complex tasks and understand the relative advantages and shortcomings between them (for example, is there a task that one method can easily achieve but the other can't? Or is there some feature of the dynamics/networks that are learnt that appears more reasonable for one than the other). Moreover, given these two largely distinct methods to train RNNs, an important question that needs to be addressed is how the mechanisms by which generalization occurs in each method differ from each other. In other words, it is not clear which aspects of the mechanisms they identified in this paper are unique to the tamed chaos method or common to more general classes of algorithms to train RNNs. This paper provides a rather detailed analysis of how their particular training method enables generalization, but, for their analysis to be more useful in understanding how the RNNs in the brain operate, showing that this is a general mechanism in RNNs would be desired.

7) It was unclear how to interpret the fact that the motor-only-training networks were also robust to temporal warping (Figure 7C). In fact, for time warping that is in between trained values, the interpolation regime, as the authors call it the motor-only-training networks were at 100% performance and one of the papers the authors cite (Lerner et al., 2014) shows that there is temporal scaling in human hemodynamic imaging mainly in the behavioral range, that is in the interpolation range. Given the chaotic nature of the networks pre-training wouldn't motor-trained-only networks have initial conditions that are almost as different for within digit than between digit? If this is true and the networks can still learn to be at 100% wouldn't that imply that the sensory training is in some sense redundant? I see the greater separation in Figure 7B but it is hard to evaluate whether the extra separation is important or overkill.

8) In general the treatment of temporal warping somewhat confusing. The text is written as if the solution to a time warped input is necessarily to generate the same trajectory running at a different speed. This doesn't have to be the case, in general all that is needed is that whatever dynamics happen, at the transition between the sensory and motor phases the within digit distance (including time warps, different utterances, etc.) be smaller than the between digit distance. The easiest way for this to be achieved is to arrive at the exact same point for different time warps. However, this is not necessary, nor is it what the network actually ends up doing (Figure 8). It was therefore very difficult for me to interpret the significance of Figure 8, that the network arrives at a mid-way solution between constant speed and constant distance. Is there something particularly interesting about this midpoint? Is there a reason it arrived at this compromise between these two possible mechanisms? Is it influenced by the way the authors generate the target trajectories by scaling?

9) The authors make one main biological prediction: "Specifically, the observation that slower stimuli yield trajectories with larger curvature radii implies that the neural population activity should exhibit larger fluctuations in their firing rates in response to slower stimuli". However, in order for that to be a true prediction at least in my mind one would need to show that this is a necessary, or at least generic property, for instance by studying multiple different types of tasks involving temporal warping, or showing somehow that without this increase in curvature radius the trajectories cannot be learned. Moreover, the effect size for this prediction shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1D appears quite mild (25% increase in range across the full span of warping).

10) Focusing on a specific set of realistic, complex stimuli and outputs is certainly a clear proof of concept of the task. Yet, the shortcoming of such an approach is that it is not immediately clear which part of the reported results are to some extent general, and what is in contrast specific to the particular implementation of the trained network (which relies on a very specific training procedure, and no doubt involves some fine-tuning). I guess what I am missing is a simplified, computational description of the underlying mechanism. Right now, I am left wondering how much details matter, and what happens when some details are changed. For instance, it seems that the specific implementation used in the paper requires that the motor action starts at a fixed time after the stimulus, and that it could not easily accommodate a variable delay between the stimulus and the motor output (e.g. specified by a go cue). Providing a simplified computational description of the mechanism, and examples of extensions/limitations would greatly improve the paper.

Thank you for submitting a revision of your article "Encoding Sensory and Motor Patterns as Time-Invariant Trajectories in Recurrent Neural Networks" for consideration by eLife.

We found the manuscript improved. In particular, the inclusion of the back propagation trained network results that came up with a similar regime to the intrinsic trajectory training was informative and useful.

However, this addition does not fully address the three summary issues raised in the original decision letter. We recognize that these are very difficult to address, and hence a complete answer may not be possible. However, we think it would be appropriate to be more explicit about the limitations of the current work/approach. As one reviewer noted, the current manuscript presents the problems as more solved than warranted and thought it would be useful to note issues that remain relatively unsolved. Your response letter takes more of an approach along these lines than the Discussion section in the revision. For example, in the biological predictions part, it would be helpful to cleanly separate previously known and relatively generic predictions, such as input driven suppression of variability and generalization being challenging, from those that are more specific to the model such as the larger curvature radii. We think this more tempered approach will make the paper more impactful, helping lay out some issues in need of future exploration

claims.claim: Robust decoding and encoding of time-varying patterns must rely on spatiotemporal dependencies inherent to the pattern.

claims.evidence: Based on logical reasoning about the nature of temporal patterns

claims.claim: Fixed-point attractor theory holds that information is stored as fixed-point attractors in recurrently connected circuits.
claims.source: One highly influential theory in neuroscience holds that information is stored as fixed-point attractors that emerge in the dynamic activity of the brain's recurrently connected circuits (Hopfield, 1982; Hopfield and Tank, 1986; Amit and Brunel, 1997; Wang, 2001).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to foundational papers in the field

claims.claim: Fixed-point attractor framework fails to capture the temporal aspect of stored information.
claims.source: Two limitations of this framework are: (1) It fails to capture the temporal aspect of stored information, thus forcing many computational models to 'spatialize' time—that is, they treat the temporal component of time-varying patterns as additional spatial dimensions (Rabiner, 1989; Waibel et al., 1989; Elman, 1990; Hinton et al., 2012; Mnih et al., 2015)
claims.evidence: Supported by citations showing how models spatialize time

claims.claim: Fixed-point attractor framework does not capture temporal invariance in brain processing.
claims.source: (2) it does not capture a fundamental feature of how the brain processes temporal information: temporal invariance. For example, humans readily recognize temporally warped—compressed or dilated—speech or music.
claims.evidence: Based on known human perceptual abilities

claims.claim: Humans readily recognize temporally warped speech or music.
claims.source: For example, humans readily recognize temporally warped—compressed or dilated—speech or music.
claims.evidence: Based on established knowledge of human perception

claims.claim: There is mounting evidence that the ability to tell time on the sub-second scale relies on the dynamics of recurrent neural networks.
claims.source: While the mechanisms that underlie the brain's ability to perform a broad range of spatiotemporal tasks in the sensory and motor domains are not known, there is mounting theoretical and experimental evidence that our ability to tell time on the sub-second scale, and represent time-varying patterns, relies on the inherent continuous dynamics, and computational potential, of recurrent neural networks (Rabinovich et al., 2008; Buonomano and Maass, 2009; Mante et al., 2013; Crowe et al., 2014; Carnevale et al., 2015; Li et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by multiple citations to theoretical and experimental studies

claims.claim: The RNN framework alleviates restrictions imposed by traditional discrete-time or fixed-point attractor models by relying on recurrent connections to implicitly maintain an ongoing memory of the pattern.
claims.source: This framework alleviates the restrictions imposed by traditional discrete-time or fixed-point attractor models, by relying on the recurrent connections to implicitly maintain an ongoing memory of the pattern.
claims.evidence: Based on theoretical understanding of RNN dynamics

claims.claim: By tuning the weights within RNN models, it is possible to robustly store and generate complex time-varying motor patterns.

claims.claim: Training shapes the basins of attraction around spoken digit-encoding trajectories based on the spatiotemporal distribution of spectral noise in the sensory input.
claims.source: In our model, this is achieved via supervised training with a common within-digit target trajectory, which exposes the spatiotemporal distribution of the spectral noise in the sensory input, and in doing so, allows for effective sampling from this distribution. Training then shapes the basins of attraction or hypertubes around the spoken digit-encoding trajectories based on this distribution, resulting in effective, recurrently-driven suppression of naturally occurring spectral noise.

claims.claim: Temporal warping (temporal invariance) is a signature and little understood feature of how the brain processes time-varying patterns.
claims.source: As mentioned above, a signature and little understood feature of how the brain processes time-varying patterns pertains to temporal warping (temporal invariance), whereby temporally compressed or dilated input signals can be identified as the same pattern.

claims.claim: One advantage of encoding time-varying stimuli as continuous neural trajectories is that it naturally addresses the problem of temporal warping.
claims.source: We hypothesized that one advantage of encoding time-varying stimuli as continuous neural trajectories, is that it naturally addresses the problem of temporal warping; specifically, that compressed or dilated stimuli generate similar neural trajectories that play out at different 'speeds' (Lerner et al., 2014; Mello et al., 2015).

claims.claim: Trajectories produced by temporally warped inputs in the sensorimotor trained RNN were closer to the reference compared to their counterparts in the reservoir or motor-trained RNN.
claims.source: Trajectories produced by temporally warped inputs in the sensorimotor trained RNN were closer to the reference compared to their counterparts in the reservoir or motor-trained RNN.

claims.claim: Tuning the recurrent weights dramatically improved the ability of the network to reproduce the same neural trajectories despite being driven by inputs at different speeds.
claims.source: In other words, tuning the recurrent weights dramatically improved the ability of the network to reproduce the same neural trajectories, despite being driven by inputs at different speeds.
claims.evidence: Based on comparison across network types

claims.claim: The trained RNN maintains a much smaller distance between trajectories across a four-fold range of temporal warping including warp factors outside the range used during training.
claims.source: In comparison to the two control networks, the trained RNN maintains a much smaller distance between trajectories across the four-fold range of temporal warping—including warp factors outside the range used during training.

claims.claim: Training during the sensory and motor epochs dramatically improves extrapolation to speeds outside the range of training speeds.
claims.source: Training during the sensory and motor epochs dramatically improves 'extrapolation'—that is generalization to speeds outside the range of training speeds

claims.claim: Training during the motor epoch alone is sufficient to produce very good interpolation generalization to novel speeds within the training set range.
claims.source: however, training during the motor epoch alone is sufficient to produce very good 'interpolation' (novel speeds within the training set range) generalization.

claims.claim: A comparison of the time-averaged linear speed of trajectories encoding digits at different warps deviates from the inverse proportional relationship in both untrained and trained networks.
claims.source: However, a comparison of the time-averaged linear speed of trajectories encoding digits at different warps deviates from this relationship in both the untrained and trained networks (Figure 8A)

claims.claim: Temporal scaling is achieved by an approximate balance of constant speed and constant distance mechanisms.
claims.source: A comparison of these measurements for the two networks to the expected values in constant speed- and constant distance trajectories, confirms that both networks produce trajectories that lie in between these two extremes.

claims.claim: At low speeds (digits spoken slowly), the trajectories are slower and longer.
claims.source: That is, temporal scaling is achieved by an approximate balance of both hypotheses, e.g., at low speeds (digits spoken slowly) the trajectories are slower and longer.
claims.evidence: Based on analysis of trajectory speeds and distances

claims.claim: Training alters the balance between constant speed and constant distance to reduce within-digit separation by modulating trajectory speeds more strongly.
claims.source: Furthermore, training alters this balance to reduce the within-digit separation, by modulating the trajectory speeds more strongly.

claims.claim: The input and recurrent subspaces in the trained network are orthogonal to one another.
claims.source: To answer this question, we first measured the relationship between the input and recurrent subspaces in the trained network, and discovered that they are orthogonal to one another (data not shown)

claims.claim: The differentiated curvature and linear velocity that modulate the angular velocity and timescales of recurrent subspace trajectories are directly shaped by input subspace dynamics.
claims.source: Ultimately, the differentiated curvature and linear velocity that modulate the angular velocity and therefore the timescales of recurrent subspace trajectories, are directly shaped by these input subspace dynamics (Rajan et al., 2010a).

claims.claim: A network trained with gradient-descent approach showed inferior interpolation and extrapolation performance compared to the network trained with 'innate' learning.
claims.source: While the interpolation and extrapolation performance of this network was inferior to the network trained with 'innate' learning (Figure 8—figure supplement 2B), the underlying mechanism was the same: warped utterances were encoded along parallel trajectories (Figure 8—figure supplement 2F–G) with warp-dependent curvature and linear velocity (Figure 8—figure supplement 2E) that subserved temporal scaling.

claims.claim: Two very different training algorithms resulted in similar solutions to the temporal invariance problem.
claims.source: Thus, two very different training algorithms resulted in similar solutions to the temporal invariance problem.
claims.evidence: Comparison of innate learning and gradient descent approaches

claims.claim: The integration of inputs at different warps separates out the resulting trajectories in the input subspace and consequently in the recurrent subspace.
claims.source: In summary, these results demonstrate that the integration of inputs at different warps separates out the resulting trajectories in the input subspace, and consequently in the recurrent subspace.

claims.claim: The network dynamics generate trajectories with warp-dependent linear velocities and curvature which appropriately modulate their angular velocity.
claims.source: In both subspaces the network dynamics generate trajectories with warp-dependent linear velocities and curvature, which appropriately modulate their angular velocity, resulting in them traversing spatially distinct yet parallel paths at warp-dependent timescales.

claims.claim: An inherent computational advantage of encoding time-varying sensory stimuli in neural trajectories is that it can naturally address the temporal invariance problem.
claims.source: This confirms the hypothesis that an inherent computational advantage of encoding time-varying sensory stimuli in neural trajectories is that it can naturally address the temporal invariance problem.
claims.evidence: Conclusion based on temporal warping analysis

claims.claim: Theoretical evidence increasingly suggests that the dynamics of recurrently connected circuits in the brain are critical to representing time-varying patterns.
claims.source: Despite our poor understanding of these processes, theoretical evidence increasingly suggests that the dynamics of recurrently connected circuits in the brain are critical to representing time-varying patterns.

claims.claim: Reservoir computing approaches propose that complex high-dimensional spatiotemporal patterns are represented in the dynamics inherent to randomly connected recurrent neural networks.
claims.source: For example, so-called reservoir computing approaches propose that complex high-dimensional spatiotemporal patterns are represented in the dynamics inherent to randomly connected recurrent neural networks (Jaeger and Haas, 2004; Buonomano and Maass, 2009; Sussillo and Abbott, 2009).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to reservoir computing literature

claims.claim: A shortcoming of reservoir computing is that the recurrent connections are not plastic and do not adapt to the task at hand.
claims.source: A shortcoming of this approach, however, is that the recurrent connections in these networks are not plastic; thus in contrast to actual cortical circuits, the random recurrent neural network (the 'reservoir') does not adapt or optimize to the task at hand.

claims.claim: Fully tapping into the computational potential of randomly connected RNNs has proven difficult because they are susceptible to chaos.
claims.source: Additionally, fully tapping into the computational potential of randomly connected RNNs has proven difficult because they are susceptible to chaos (Sompolinsky et al., 1988; Wallace et al., 2013).

claims.claim: Experience-dependent plasticity could reshape the dynamics of reservoir RNNs to qualitatively improve representations by endowing them with generalization, sensory-motor association, and temporal invariance.
claims.source: Here, we extend these results to better understand well-known aspects of the brain's ability to represent time-varying sensory and motor patterns—we demonstrate how experience-dependent plasticity could reshape the dynamics of reservoir RNNs to qualitatively improve representations by endowing them with such essential properties as generalization to novel exemplars, sensory-motor association and transformation, and temporal invariance.

claims.claim: Previous models of temporal scaling have enlisted neural and synaptic dynamics to achieve temporal invariance of both sensory stimuli and motor responses.
claims.source: Previous models of temporal scaling have enlisted neural and synaptic dynamics to achieve temporal invariance of both sensory stimuli (Gütig and Sompolinsky, 2009) and the generation of motor responses (Murray and Escola, 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior models

claims.claim: In the Gutig and Sompolinsky model, temporally invariant recognition is based on a synaptic shunting mechanism where the effective integration time is modulated by total conductance of afferent synapses.
claims.source: In the model proposed by Gutig and Sompolinsky, temporally invariant recognition of compressed and dilated sensory stimuli is based on a synaptic shunting mechanism, wherein the effective integration time of a post-synaptic cell is modulated by the total conductance of its afferent synapses, which changes as a monotonic function of the input warp—thus temporal invariance is ultimately reduced to a cellular property.

claims.claim: In the current model, temporal invariance emerges from a network property: the formation of parallel neural trajectories traversed at different speeds.
claims.source: In contrast, in the model described here temporal invariance emerges from a network property: the formation of parallel neural trajectories traversed at different speeds.

claims.claim: The capacity for parallel trajectories at different speeds is the consequence of scale-dependent angular velocities of the encoding trajectories.
claims.source: While the formation of such trajectories may be surprising given the sensitivity and nonlinear nature of RNNs, we show that this capacity is the consequence of scale-dependent angular velocities of the encoding trajectories.

claims.claim: The property of scale-dependent angular velocities stems from leaky integration of scaled inputs and input-driven suppression of chaotic recurrent activity.
claims.source: This property of RNN encoding, which is observable to a lesser extent even in reservoir networks (Figure 8D), stems from its leaky integration of scaled inputs (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B) and the input-driven suppression of its chaotic recurrent activity (Rajan et al., 2010a).
claims.evidence: Explanation with figure references and citation

claims.claim: Network training enhances scale-dependent angular velocities by suppressing recurrent amplification of scale-driven deviations in encoding trajectories.
claims.source: Indeed, network training enhances this property by suppressing recurrent amplification of scale-driven deviations in the encoding trajectories, producing proximal, parallel within-digit trajectories with linear velocities that are more strongly scale-dependent (Figure 8D, Figure 8—figure supplements 1C, 2E and G).

claims.claim: Training across both sensory and motor epochs improves interpolation and extrapolation generalization and strongly enhances cross-utterance and cross-speaker generalization.
claims.source: Nevertheless, it remains the case that training across both the sensory and motor epochs, not only improves interpolation and extrapolation generalization, but also strongly enhances cross-utterance and cross-speaker generalization (Figure 1C).

claims.claim: Training an RNN reveals a computationally powerful pattern recognition regime that helps generalize the encoding of learned time-varying patterns to novel exemplars.
claims.source: Our results also demonstrate how training an RNN reveals a computationally powerful pattern recognition regime, one that helps generalize the encoding of learned time-varying patterns to novel exemplars.

claims.claim: Recognizing different instances of the same digit as one and the same while discriminating between different digits requires networks to differentially sculpt within and between class trajectories.
claims.source: As stated earlier, recognizing different instances of the same digit as one and the same, while discriminating between different digits requires that networks actively and differentially sculpt the within and between class trajectories—the separation between trajectories representing similar patterns must be kept to a minimum, while that between trajectories representing different patterns must be amplified.

claims.claim: Untrained random recurrent networks (reservoir networks) in the critical regime amplify the separation between trajectories representing similar patterns more strongly than between different patterns.
claims.source: A previous study has analytically shown that untrained random recurrent networks (reservoir networks) process inputs in one of three computational regimes: a chaotic regime, wherein any separation between trajectories is strongly amplified by the network's chaotic dynamics; a regime with weak recurrent weights that is input-dominated with little computational power; and a critical regime wherein the input and internal dynamics are balanced (Bertschinger and Natschläger, 2004). Here, we show that training alters these regimes in very different ways (Figure 5). Crucially, relative to the separation between the input patterns, reservoir networks in the critical regime amplify the separation between trajectories representing similar patterns more strongly than between different patterns.
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 5 with citation to prior work

claims.claim: Trained networks separate trajectories according to the patterns they are representing.
claims.source: In contrast, trained networks separate trajectories according to the patterns they are representing (Figure 5A).

claims.claim: Tuning the recurrent weights reshapes the internal dynamics of the network, enabling it to redirect or suppress deviations from the target trajectories.
claims.source: Tuning the recurrent weights reshapes the internal dynamics of the network, enabling it to redirect or suppress deviations from the target trajectories (Figure 6).

claims.claim: The model predicts that neural trajectories will be stable in response to local perturbations potentially administered through optogenetic stimulation.
claims.source: Three experimentally tractable predictions emerge from the above results. First, neural trajectories will be stable in response to local perturbations potentially administered through optogenetic stimulation.

claims.claim: The model predicts that neural trajectories elicited during sensory stimuli will be more resistant to perturbations than neural trajectories during the motor epoch of sensory-motor tasks.
claims.source: Importantly, and in agreement with an earlier analysis (Rajan et al., 2010a), the neural trajectories elicited during sensory stimuli will be more resistant to perturbations than the neural trajectories unfolding during the motor epoch of sensory-motor tasks.
claims.evidence: Prediction based on model results with citation

claims.claim: The model predicts that trajectories in sensory areas will diverge more when presented stimuli composed of artificial or unfamiliar spectral noise patterns.
claims.source: A second prediction, which to the best of our knowledge is a novel one, relates to the structure of noise. Specifically, trained networks fail at generalizing to unfamiliar spectral noise patterns, thereby generating the prediction that trajectories in sensory areas will diverge more when presented stimuli composed of artificial or unfamiliar spectral noise patterns.
claims.evidence: Prediction based on spectral noise analysis

claims.claim: The model predicts that slower stimuli yield trajectories with larger curvature radii, implying neural population activity should exhibit larger fluctuations in firing rates in response to slower stimuli.
claims.source: Third, and most specifically, the model predicts a clear neural correlate of the encoding of temporally scaled stimuli—the observation that slower stimuli yield trajectories with larger curvature radii implies that the neural population activity should exhibit larger fluctuations in their firing rates in response to slower stimuli; In other words, at the neuronal level the range of minimal to maximal firing rate should be larger (Figure 8—figure supplements 1D and 2D).
claims.evidence: Prediction based on trajectory analysis shown in figures

claims.claim: The learning rule used in the model, coupled with its requirement of an explicit target for each recurrent unit, is biologically implausible.
claims.source: Most notably, how can the recurrent synaptic strengths be tuned to develop stable trajectories in a biologically plausible manner? The learning rule used here, coupled with its requirement of an explicit target for each recurrent unit, make it biologically implausible.

claims.claim: It is conceivable that arbitrary yet locally-stable encoding trajectories may emerge from unsupervised learning.
claims.source: However, while it is important that the sensorimotor representations are encoded as locally stable trajectories, the structure of the target trajectories themselves are essentially arbitrary. It is therefore conceivable that arbitrary yet locally-stable encoding trajectories may emerge from unsupervised learning.

claims.claim: It is not clear if training over a range of sensory stimuli speeds represents a biologically plausible scenario.
claims.source: A second related issue is that to achieve strong temporal invariance, our model had to be trained over a range of sensory stimuli speeds. Again, it is not clear if this would represent a biologically plausible scenario

claims.claim: It will be important for future research to determine if the ability to recognize stimuli independent of speed is learned through experience.
claims.source: to help address this question, it will be important for future research to determine if the ability to recognize stimuli independent of speed is learned through experience.

claims.claim: The computational potential of continuous time RNNs in high-gain regimes has long been recognized but has been challenging to tap into because of their inherently chaotic behavior and difficulties in training them.
claims.source: The computational potential of continuous time RNNs in high-gain regimes has long been recognized, but it has been challenging to tap into this potential because of their inherently chaotic behavior and the difficulties in training them (Bengio et al., 1994; Pearlmutter, 1995).

claims.claim: A further feature of trained RNNs is their ability to encode spatiotemporal objects, perform complex sensorimotor tasks, and address the problem of temporal warping.
claims.source: Here, we establish that a further feature of trained RNNs is their ability to not only encode spatiotemporal objects, but also to perform complex sensorimotor tasks and address the long-standing problem of temporal warping.

claims.claim: These results are consistent with the proposal that spatiotemporal objects are not encoded as fixed-point attractors but as locally stable neural trajectories (dynamic attractors).
claims.source: These results are consistent with the proposal that that spatiotemporal objects are not encoded as fixed-point attractors, but as locally stable neural trajectories (dynamic attractors).

results.result: A trained RNN successfully performs a sensorimotor transcription task, converting spoken digits (0-9) into handwritten digit patterns with 98.7% accuracy on novel test stimuli, demonstrating generalization across speakers and utterances.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C20, C21, C38, C39, and C41 collectively demonstrate successful transcription performance. The quantitative performance metric (98.7% on 410 novel stimuli, C41) evaluated by an independent CNN classifier provides strong evidence. Generalization to novel utterances and speakers (C39) with visual confirmation (Figure 1B, Video 1) supports the robustness of the result.

results.result: Training transforms chaotic reservoir dynamics into stable neural trajectories that encode time-varying sensory and motor patterns as 'hypertubes' in phase space, with trajectories for the same digit converging while different digits remain well-separated.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C62 provide detailed trajectory analysis showing that training reduces within-digit variability while maintaining between-digit separation (Figures 3, 4). The conceptual framework of hypertubes (C60-C62) is supported by PCA visualizations. Claims C29-C31 establish the computational requirements that are demonstrably met by the trained network.

results.result: Training the RNN significantly decreases within-digit trajectory distances during both sensory and motor epochs while preserving large between-digit separations, achieved through supervised learning with common target trajectories for each digit.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C67 provide quantitative measurements (Figure 4A) showing decreased within-digit distances without loss of between-digit separation. Claims C71-C74 explain the mechanism through the training paradigm. The result is well-supported by both empirical measurements and mechanistic explanation.

results.result: Temporal invariance emerges naturally in trained RNNs through the formation of parallel neural trajectories with appropriately modulated angular velocities, enabling recognition of the same digit spoken at different speeds across a four-fold range of temporal warping.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C113 provide strong empirical evidence from temporal warping experiments (Figures 7, 8) showing maintained trajectory similarity across warp factors. Claims C4, C134, C135 explain the mechanism through modulated angular velocities. The convergence of empirical observation and mechanistic explanation strongly supports this major finding.

results.result: Temporal scaling in RNNs is achieved through a balance of constant speed and constant distance mechanisms, where trajectories at different temporal warps exhibit warp-dependent linear velocities and curvature that modulate their angular velocity.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C118 provide quantitative measurements (Figure 8A, 8D) showing deviations from simple inverse proportionality and the balance between mechanisms. Claims C121, C124, C125 explain how input and recurrent subspace dynamics shape this behavior. The detailed mechanistic analysis with supporting data provides strong support.

results.result: Control experiments demonstrate that reservoir networks achieve only 20% performance and motor-only trained networks achieve 71% performance, confirming the importance of sensory epoch training for the full 98.7% performance.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C46 provide clear performance comparisons (Figure 1C) across three network types with mechanistic explanations for the differences. The control experiments are well-designed and the performance differences are substantial, strongly supporting the importance of recurrent weight training during the sensory epoch.

results.result: Trained RNNs exhibit robust dynamic attractors during the motor epoch that recover from perturbations, with sensory epoch trajectories showing greater stability due to external input stabilization.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C54 are supported by perturbation experiments (Figure 2) showing trajectory recovery and graceful performance degradation. The differential stability between sensory and motor epochs is demonstrated quantitatively (Figure 2C) and explained mechanistically through input stabilization.

results.result: Training compresses the eigenspectrum of the recurrent weight matrix, bringing eigenvalues with real parts greater than one closer to one, consistent with increased network stability.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C76 are supported by eigenspectrum analysis (Figure 4B) with appropriate citations to prior theoretical work. However, the authors acknowledge that interpretation is not straightforward due to network nonlinearity and mixed autonomous/driven operation, which appropriately tempers the conclusion.

results.result: Network performance depends critically on input amplitude, with optimal discrimination occurring at intermediate amplitudes (0.5-5) where both external input and internal dynamics shape trajectories, while extreme amplitudes either dominate internal dynamics or render the network insensitive to input.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C94 provide comprehensive parametric analysis (Figure 5) showing how input amplitude affects within-digit and between-digit distances, dimensionality, and discrimination. The systematic exploration across amplitudes with both trained and untrained networks provides strong support for the optimal regime identification.

results.result: Trained RNNs suppress natural spectral noise through recurrent dynamics that rotate the recurrent subspace to be anti-correlated with input subspace deviations, but fail to generalize to artificial noise patterns with unfamiliar structure.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C105 provide detailed analysis (Figure 6) using novel subspace decomposition methods showing selective suppression of natural vs. artificial noise. The progressive increase in trajectory distances from trained to untrained to shuffled to orthogonal noise (C100) provides strong evidence. The mechanistic explanation through subspace rotation (C105) is well-supported.

results.result: Two different training algorithms (innate learning and gradient descent via BPTT) produce similar solutions to temporal invariance through parallel trajectories with modulated angular velocities, though gradient descent shows inferior interpolation/extrapolation performance.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C123 demonstrate convergence of mechanisms across training methods (Figure 8—figure supplement 2), supporting generality of the temporal invariance solution. However, the inferior performance of BPTT-trained networks (C122) suggests the innate learning approach may have advantages. The comparison strengthens confidence in the mechanism while acknowledging method-dependent performance differences.

results.result: The RNN training procedure uses supervised 'innate learning' where recurrent units learn to reproduce target trajectories from the untrained network in the presence of noise and varying initial conditions, followed by separate output unit training.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C36 clearly describe the training methodology with appropriate citations. The separation of recurrent and output training (C35-C36) is justified both computationally and with biological precedent (C37). This is methodological description rather than a novel finding.

results.result: The model uses a continuous-time firing-rate RNN with sparse random recurrent connections initialized in a high-gain regime (g=1.6), with the task divided into sensory and motor epochs.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C28 describe the model architecture and task structure, which are clearly specified in the methods and figures. This is methodological description supported by standard citations and clear documentation.

results.result: A deep CNN trained on MNIST and fine-tuned on stenciled digits was used to objectively evaluate RNN transcription performance, achieving 98.7% accuracy on 410 novel test stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C41 describe the evaluation methodology and report the key performance metric. The use of an independent classifier provides objective assessment. This is a methodological choice that enables the main performance result but is itself a minor contribution.

results.result: The property of scale-dependent angular velocities stems from leaky integration of scaled inputs and input-driven suppression of chaotic activity, with training enhancing this property by suppressing recurrent amplification of scale-driven deviations.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C138 provide mechanistic explanation for temporal invariance with supporting data (Figure 8D, supplements). The explanation connects network properties (leaky integration, chaos suppression) to the observed behavior. The citation to prior work (C136) and demonstration that the property exists even in reservoirs but is enhanced by training (C137) provides strong support.

results.result: The model generates three experimentally testable predictions: (1) neural trajectories will be stable to perturbations with sensory trajectories more resistant than motor trajectories, (2) trajectories will diverge more for artificial/unfamiliar spectral noise, and (3) slower stimuli will produce larger firing rate ranges.
results.evaluation: Claims C144-C147 present clear, testable predictions derived from the model results. These are appropriately framed as predictions rather than established facts. The predictions follow logically from the demonstrated model properties (perturbation stability, spectral noise selectivity, trajectory curvature analysis).

results.result: The authors acknowledge limitations including biological implausibility of the learning rule and uncertainty about whether training across multiple speeds is biologically realistic, suggesting future work on unsupervised learning and experience-dependent temporal invariance.
results.evaluation: Claims C148-C151 represent appropriate acknowledgment of model limitations and suggestions for future work. These are honest assessments of the model's constraints rather than results per se. The speculation about unsupervised learning (C149) is appropriately tentative.

results.result: The balance between sensory and motor processing modes depends on recurrent weight strength and external drive magnitude, with high-gain regimes enabling both high-dimensional sensory discrimination and autonomous motor generation.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C84 explain the computational requirements for dual sensory-motor function and how the model satisfies them. The explanation is logical and supported by the parametric input amplitude analysis (Figure 5). However, this is primarily conceptual framework and interpretation rather than novel empirical findings.

results.result: Training reveals a computationally powerful pattern recognition regime where networks differentially sculpt within-class and between-class trajectory separations, contrasting with reservoir networks that amplify within-class separation more than between-class separation.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C143 synthesize findings about how training improves discrimination, with C141 citing prior analytical work on reservoir regimes and C142 showing trained networks behave differently (Figure 5A). This represents an important conceptual advance in understanding trained vs. untrained RNN dynamics.

results.result: The authors establish context by reviewing prior work on temporal processing, fixed-point attractors, and RNN approaches, identifying the gap that sensory discrimination with RNNs remains unexplored despite success with motor pattern generation.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C14 provide literature review and motivation. These are appropriately cited statements about prior work and known phenomena that establish context. They are not novel findings but rather background that frames the study's contributions.

results.result: The authors establish that sensory and motor areas interact in the brain and have disparate computational requirements, with no previous models showing a single network can satisfy both requirements.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C19 provide biological and computational context with appropriate citations (C15-C16) and establish the novelty of the current work (C19). These are literature review statements that motivate the study rather than novel findings.

results.result: The authors position their work as extending reservoir computing approaches by demonstrating how experience-dependent plasticity can reshape RNN dynamics to improve representations with generalization, sensory-motor association, and temporal invariance.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C131 provide discussion context, reviewing reservoir computing limitations (C129-C130) and positioning the current contributions (C131). This is appropriate framing of the work's significance relative to prior approaches.

results.result: The current model's mechanism for temporal invariance (parallel trajectories at different speeds) differs fundamentally from prior models like Gütig and Sompolinsky's synaptic shunting mechanism, representing a network-level rather than cellular-level solution.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C134 appropriately contrast the current approach with prior models, highlighting the conceptual difference between network-level and cellular-level mechanisms. This comparison helps establish the novelty and significance of the current findings.

results.result: The RNN operates in fundamentally different regimes during sensory and motor epochs, with external input partially suppressing internal dynamics during sensory processing while motor processing is entirely autonomous.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C50 describe the operational modes of the network with appropriate citations (C47). This is important for understanding the model but represents characterization of the model's behavior rather than a novel empirical finding requiring extensive validation.

results.result: The finding that training improves discrimination is contextualized within the established framework of experience-dependent plasticity in cortical circuits.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C64 connect the computational findings to neuroscience literature on cortical plasticity. C63 provides appropriate biological context with citations, while C64 states the computational finding. This represents appropriate contextualization rather than a standalone result.

results.result: Successful formation of dynamic attractors requires low within-digit separation at the end of the sensory epoch and substantially larger between-digit than within-digit separation to ensure robust sensory-motor transitions.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C70 provide mechanistic explanation for attractor formation based on trajectory analysis. This represents important insight into the requirements for successful sensory-motor coupling, though it is derived from the trajectory analysis rather than being independently validated.

results.result: The work establishes that trained RNNs in high-gain regimes can encode spatiotemporal objects, perform complex sensorimotor tasks, and address temporal warping, consistent with dynamic attractor rather than fixed-point attractor encoding.
results.evaluation: Claims C152-C154 provide concluding synthesis of the work's contributions. These represent appropriate summary statements of the main findings rather than new results. The framing in terms of dynamic vs. fixed-point attractors (C154) provides important conceptual context.
